questions.question: What is event delegation and why is it useful?
questions.title: Event Delegation
questions.direct_answer: Event delegation attaches ONE listener on a parent element instead of many on children, exploiting event bubbling: a listener on the parent fires for events on any descendant. The handler uses e.target (the actual clicked element) to decide what to do. Benefits: fewer listeners (memory/perf), works for dynamically added children (no re-binding), and simplifies teardown.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The capture/bubble pipeline (the full model): an event dispatched on a node first travels DOWN (capture: window → document → ... → target's parent), then hits the target (target phase), then travels UP (bubble: parent → ... → window). addEventListener(type, fn, true) listens on the capture leg — useful for intercepting before child handlers (and for the rare non-bubbling events). Delegation uses the bubble leg by default.

stopPropagation vs stopImmediatePropagation (the edge cases): stopPropagation halts further ancestors from seeing the event, but other handlers ON the same element still run. stopImmediatePropagation also cancels remaining same-element handlers. In delegated handlers, calling stopPropagation prevents outer delegation layers from reacting — usually intentional in nested-delegation designs.

The React connection (the fact that closes the loop): React's synthetic event system IS delegation — React 16 attaches one listener per event type at the document root (17+: at the root container), then maps events back to component handlers. This is why 10,000 onClick props cost far less than 10,000 native listeners, and why events on portals still bubble through the React tree (React's synthetic bubbling follows the React tree, not the DOM tree).
